headline: Friendly foxes have fewer of certain brain cells

sources.title: From wild to mild: Friendly foxes show changes in brain region (Cornell Chronicle)
Brain Circuit Pruned to Make Wild Foxes Friendly (Neuroscience News)
Fox experiment is replaying domestication in fast-forward (Science News)

chunks.text: Foxes [[bred]] to be friendly have fewer of a certain kind of [[brain cell]] than foxes bred to be [[aggressive]], a new study says. Bred means people chose which animals had babies. The study {{came out}} on November 2, 2026, in the [[science journal]] Current Biology. A team at Cornell University {{set out}} to learn how the brain changes when a wild animal becomes [[tame]], or calm around people.

chunks.text: The foxes are part of a famous experiment that began on [[fur farms]] in Siberia, Russia, in the late 1950s. Some foxes {{stood out}} because they were friendlier toward workers. Only the friendliest foxes had babies, and they {{passed on}} this behavior. After six [[generations]], scientists {{ended up}} with [[pups]] that wanted to be with humans. [[Floppy ears]] and shorter [[snouts]], or noses, {{showed up}} too. In 2017, a science magazine reported that the foxes {{rolled over}} for [[belly rubs]] but still did not [[follow commands]] like dogs.

My dog rolls over when he wants attention. Many cats roll over and show their bellies. In 2017, a science magazine reported that the foxes rolled over for belly rubs.

chunks.text: Scientists in Russia sent the team nine [[preserved]] brains: three from tame foxes, three from aggressive foxes, and three from wild foxes. The team studied [[thin slices]] from a small area [[at the base of]] the brain. In earlier work on mice, scientists used light to {{turn on}} certain brain cells there, and the mouse would attack another. The tame foxes {{turned out}} to have fewer of this same kind of cell than aggressive foxes.

chunks.text: The study does not [[prove]] that these cells make a fox friendly. It used only nine brains. The link between these cells and attacks is also based on mice, not foxes. The scientists do not yet know how the difference {{came about}}. Next, they want to {{figure out}} why breeding changes this part of the brain. One team member may {{look into}} how fox [[genes]] affect these cells.

mainIdea.s: Foxes bred to be tame have fewer of a certain brain cell than foxes bred to be aggressive. The study used only nine brains, and scientists still need to learn why the difference exists.
mainIdea.why: Tame foxes turned out to have fewer of these cells. The study is very small, and the next step is to figure out why.

mainIdea.s: Scientists have shown that one type of cell makes every fox friendly or dangerous. Removing those cells in a Russian experiment calmed angry animals within only six generations.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the study does not prove that these cells make a fox friendly. Nobody removed any cells, and the link to aggression is based on mice.

mainIdea.s: A Russian fur farm has closed after decades of raising silver foxes for sale as pets. Workers must now find new homes for hundreds of animals, and a court will decide who pays the costs.
mainIdea.why: This is about a study of nine fox brains. It found that tame foxes turned out to have fewer of certain brain cells.

lines.text: Did you see the story about the friendly foxes in Russia?
Friendly foxes? I thought foxes were wild animals.
These are different. Scientists started breeding them to be tame in the late 1950s. After six generations, they {{ended up}} with pups that wanted to be with people.
Did the foxes change in other ways?
Yes. Floppy ears and shorter noses {{showed up}} too.
[[Come to think of it]], I once saw a photo of a fox that looked like a dog.
Some foxes even {{rolled over}} for belly rubs.
So I could have one as a pet and teach it tricks?
[[Dream on]]. Even in 2017 they still didn't follow commands like dogs.
Okay, so what's the new part?
A study {{came out}} on November 2. The tame foxes {{turned out}} to have fewer of a certain brain cell than aggressive foxes.
In mice, when scientists {{turn on}} those cells, the mouse attacks another mouse.
So they found the friendly switch in the brain?
[[I wouldn't go that far]]. They only had nine brains, so [[let's not get ahead of ourselves]].
Nine? That's tiny. Do they know how the difference {{came about}}?
Not yet. They want to {{figure out}} why breeding changes that part of the brain.
Well, I still want a fox.
